passage:
Monday: At the school canteen, Divyansh patted his empty pockets. "Lend me twenty for a samosa? We're best friends, na." Pradeep handed over his coins. The twenty never came back.
Thursday: Divyansh asked again, this time for cricket stickers. Pradeep's stomach went tight. It would be the fourth loan this month, and not one had been paid back. "Not today," he said softly. "I'm saving for a kite." Divyansh frowned. "Some best friend you are."
The next Tuesday, Divyansh asked a third time that week. That evening Pradeep told Mummy everything while she folded clothes. She put the shirts down, listened to the whole story, and said, "You were right to say no. Let's work out together what you can say if he asks again."

qa.q: What did Divyansh want to buy on Monday?
qa.a: A samosa from the school canteen.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when Divyansh asked for stickers?
qa.a: He felt used and uneasy; his stomach went tight because none of the loans came back, yet he was scared of losing his friend.

qa.q: What small steps helped Pradeep, and what could come next?
qa.a: He said a polite "not today" and then told Mummy; next, they can plan calm words for the next time Divyansh asks.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Pradeep's refusal?
qa.a: Divyansh seems to feel let down and uses "best friend" to push, without noticing that the unpaid loans have made Pradeep feel used.

grounding: A child whose friend borrows again and again with "we are best friends" feels used, refuses politely and turns to a parent.

passage: Sachin, sit here, kanna. You asked why I told you to say no to your friend. When your Paati was a girl in our lane in Madurai, my friend Leela and I did everything together. Every week she said, "Ganga, give me your two annas, we are best friends, I'll return it." She never did. I felt cheated, yet I was afraid she would stop playing with me. One day my tin box was empty and I cried behind the well. My Appa found me there, and I told him everything. He did not scold. He said, "A real friend can hear a no." The next time Leela asked, I said, "Not this week, Leela," in my politest voice. She sulked for two days. Then she came back with her hopscotch stone as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: Where did young Ganga cry when her tin box was empty?
qa.a: Behind the well.

qa.q: Why was young Ganga afraid to refuse Leela?
qa.a: She felt cheated by the unpaid loans but was scared that Leela would stop playing with her.

qa.q: Which choice in Paati's story changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Telling her Appa and then giving Leela a polite "not this week"; it stopped the lending without a fight.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt when Ganga said no?
qa.a: Leela was probably surprised and annoyed, since she sulked for two days, but she came back to play, so the friendship still mattered to her.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a childhood friend who kept borrowing on the claim of best friendship, and how a polite refusal and telling a parent helped.

passage: I'm Raghav, and last month my little sister Rashmi turned six. For weeks I had been dropping coins into a steel box for a comic I really wanted. The day before her birthday I stood in the stationery shop with the comic in one hand and a butterfly hair clip in the other. Nobody told me what to choose. Amma had even said the money was mine to keep. I bought the clip. When Rashmi tore off the paper, she squealed, clipped it on at once and wore it to bed, even though it poked her ear. I lay awake grinning in the dark. The comic would have been finished in a day. That squeal is still in my head.

qa.q: What did Raghav buy for Rashmi?
qa.a: A butterfly hair clip.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel after seeing Rashmi's reaction?
qa.a: Raghav felt joyful and proud, lying awake grinning, because giving the clip felt bigger than the comic would have.

qa.q: Why did this gift feel so good, and what could have spoiled it?
qa.a: It was Raghav's own choice, since Amma said the money was Raghav's to keep; if someone had forced the gift, it would have felt like pressure instead of joy.

qa.q: How did Rashmi experience the gift?
qa.a: Rashmi was thrilled; she squealed and wore the clip to bed even though it poked her ear.

grounding: A child freely spends saved pocket money on a gift for a little sister and finds the joy of giving bigger than buying for self.

passage:
Art-class note, Saturday
After class, Anirban stayed back to ask if he could buy one of the painted clay diyas from our school stall. He counted out his own pocket money on my table, coin by coin. His friend Naveen nudged him: "Buy the robot keyring instead, yaar!" Anirban shook his head. "It's for Mishti, my little sister. She's four, she loves shiny things." When I asked whether someone at home had told him to buy it, he looked puzzled. "No, I just want to."
He chose the blue one, wrapped it in newspaper himself and grinned all the way to the gate.
I told him it was a generous choice because it was his own. I also sent a short line home so his parents would know the gift came from his savings and his heart.

qa.q: What did Anirban buy for Mishti?
qa.a: The blue painted clay diya.

qa.q: What does Anirban's grin at the gate suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He felt happy and proud; giving something to Mishti mattered more to him than the robot keyring.

qa.q: How did the art teacher support Anirban's choice?
qa.a: They praised it as generous because it was his own idea, and sent a line home so his parents knew.

qa.q: What would change if someone at home had ordered Anirban to buy Mishti a present?
qa.a: The gift might feel like a duty instead of a pleasure; his grin came from choosing it himself.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy freely spending his pocket money on a gift for his little sister and enjoying it more than buying for himself.

passage:
Sunday: Papa handed Mehak a tin box with a slot on top. "Your pocket money goes in here. Mummy and I won't count it," he said. Mehak stood a little taller. She kept a notebook and wrote down every coin.
Wednesday: On the walk home she bought two ice lollies, one for herself and one for her friend Jagdish, and dropped the change into a drain. Now the notebook and the box did not match. She thought about rubbing out the numbers. Instead, at dinner, she mumbled, "Papa, I lost some change. It was my fault."
Papa nodded slowly. "Thank you for telling me."
The next Sunday he gave her the tiny key to the box. "You told me the hard part yourself, so this is yours." Mehak held it tight.

qa.q: What did Papa give Mehak the next Sunday?
qa.a: The tiny key to the box.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when the notebook and the box did not match?
qa.a: She felt worried and guilty, even tempted to rub out the numbers, before choosing to tell Papa.

qa.q: What does Mehak's choice show about keeping trust?
qa.a: Owning up to the lost change, even though it was a mistake, made Papa trust her more, not less.

qa.q: How does Papa see Mehak's confession?
qa.a: Papa sees it as proof she can be trusted with her own money, so he thanks her and hands over the key.

grounding: A girl whose parents do not count her savings feels trusted and keeps that trust by honestly reporting a mistake.

passage: Aadhya, you keep asking why I never peep into your money jar. Let me tell you. When your Nani was small, my Amma gave me a clay gullak and said, "Neelam, this is yours. I won't shake it to check." I felt so grown-up. I had promised it was for new school sandals. But at the Dussehra fair I cracked it open early and spent everything on a tin whistle that broke by evening. I sat on the step and cried, not for the whistle, but because Amma had trusted me. I could have said a thief took it. That night I told her the truth instead. She was quiet for a long time. The next week she brought a new gullak from the potter. "You told me yourself," she said. "That is worth more than the coins."

qa.q: What did young Neelam buy at the Dussehra fair?
qa.a: A tin whistle that broke by evening.

qa.q: Why did young Neelam cry on the step that evening?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty, not about the whistle, but because Amma had trusted her with the gullak.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Telling Amma the truth that night instead of blaming a thief; it kept Amma's trust and earned a new gullak.

qa.q: How might Neelam's Amma have felt when she heard the truth?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed at first, since she went quiet, but also touched that Neelam told her honestly.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how her mother trusted her with a savings pot and how honestly reporting a mistake kept that trust.

passage:
In their flat in Pune, Sachin had been stuck on the castle level for three evenings. Then a player named Zubin joined his team, showed him a hidden bridge and shielded him through the last fight. They won! 🎉
"gg bro, same time tomorrow?" Zubin typed.
Sachin's chest felt warm. It was like having an older friend. When Zubin asked, "which city u in?", Sachin paused, then typed, "not sharing that, sorry 🙂".
After dinner he turned the screen towards Mama. "This is Zubin. He helped me win. Can I keep playing with him?"
Mama watched a whole round beside him. "Keep it in the game chat, and show me if anything ever feels odd," she said. Sachin nodded and logged off happily.

qa.q: How did Zubin help Sachin win?
qa.a: He showed Sachin a hidden bridge and shielded him through the last fight.

qa.q: What does Sachin's warm chest suggest about his feelings for Zubin?
qa.a: He feels close and grateful, as if he has found an older friend.

qa.q: Which two choices kept Sachin safe while he enjoyed the friendship?
qa.a: He refused to share his city and showed Mama who he plays with.

qa.q: What would change if Zubin kept pushing to know Sachin's city?
qa.a: That would be a warning sign; Sachin should stop chatting and tell Mama straight away.

grounding: A boy enjoys a kind player who helps him win but keeps his city private and lets his mother know who he plays with.

passage:
"Didi, look! Owlet just gave me his extra sword so I could beat the boss!"
Jasleen leaned over the sofa. "Who's Owlet?"
"A player. He's so nice. We've played every evening this week. He says I'm the best teammate he's ever had."
"Nice. What do you two talk about?"
"Just the game. Oh, today he asked my real name."
"Did you tell him?"
"No. I typed 'just call me C'." Chetan grinned. "Was that right?"
"Very right. Playing with game friends is fine, but your real name, school and photos stay with you."
"Can I still play with him?"
"Let's show Mummy his profile tonight so she knows who you play with."
After dinner Mummy scrolled through the chat with Chetan. "All fine. Keep it just like this," she said.

qa.q: What did Owlet give Chetan?
qa.a: His extra sword, so Chetan could beat the boss.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel about Owlet?
qa.a: He feels excited and close to Owlet, and proud that Owlet calls him the best teammate.

qa.q: What did Jasleen advise, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: To keep his real name, school and photos private and show Mummy the profile, so Chetan can enjoy the friendship safely.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see her brother's new game friend?
qa.a: Jasleen is glad Chetan is having fun but stays watchful, so she wants Mummy to know who he plays with.

grounding: A boy feels close to a kind online player but keeps his real name private and lets his parent see who he plays with.

passage: This is Arohi, and last Saturday I learned something about the mute button. I was playing an online football game with my cousin Nitin watching over my shoulder. I missed an easy goal, and a player called RexKing started typing: "useless noob", "uninstall", "ur team hates u". My face went hot. My fingers were already typing something worse back. Nitin said, "Arohi, that's what RexKing wants." I stopped. I pressed mute, then block, and the chat went quiet. Then I went to Papa and showed him the screen. Papa reported the account with me and said I had handled it smartly. My hands were still shaky, but I felt proud too.

qa.q: What did RexKing type after Arohi missed the goal?
qa.a: "useless noob", "uninstall" and "ur team hates u".

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when the insults came?
qa.a: Arohi felt angry and hurt; the hot face and fingers typing something worse show the urge to hit back.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than replying, and why?
qa.a: Muting, blocking and telling Papa; the chat went quiet, while insults back would only have kept it going.

qa.q: What was RexKing likely hoping for?
qa.a: RexKing was probably hoping for an angry reply to keep the fight going; muting gave nothing back.

grounding: A child insulted by a stranger in an online game feels hot anger but mutes, blocks and tells a parent instead of trading insults.

passage:
Computer club log, Thursday
During free play, Chinmay joined an online kart race. Another racer began sending insults in the open chat, calling him slow and stupid. I watched his ears turn red and his hands press hard on the keys. He typed a long reply in capitals. Elizabeth, sitting next to him, whispered, "Don't send it." He held his finger over Enter for a moment, then deleted the message.
He came to my desk, still breathing fast. Together we muted, blocked and reported the racer. I told Chinmay that stopping was the harder and smarter move. I also emailed his mother so they could talk it through at home.
He spent the rest of the session building a track with Elizabeth.

qa.q: What did the other racer call Chinmay?
qa.a: Slow and stupid.

qa.q: What do Chinmay's red ears and hard key presses suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was furious and humiliated and wanted to hit back with insults of his own.

qa.q: What did the club supervisor do next that helped?
qa.a: They muted, blocked and reported the racer with Chinmay, praised him for stopping, and emailed his mother.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth see Chinmay's long reply?
qa.a: Elizabeth could see it would only make things worse, so she quietly urged him not to send it.

grounding: A club log shows a boy insulted in an online race who, though angry, deletes his reply, blocks the player and tells an adult.

passage:
Keerthana was building a sweet shop in her block game when a message popped up: "Want 5000 free gems? Just send ur password and I'll load them 😊"
Five thousand! She could finally buy the golden roof. Her fingers hovered over the keys. Then she remembered her cousin Deepak saying that real games never ask for passwords. Her stomach flipped. This was not luck. This was bait.
She did not reply. She carried the tablet straight to the kitchen, where Amma was chopping onions. Amma wiped her hands, read the message and sat with her while they blocked and reported the player and changed the password.
"You came to me right away," Amma said, hugging her. "That was exactly right."

qa.q: What did the message ask Keerthana to send?
qa.a: Her password.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she first saw the offer?
qa.a: She felt excited about the golden roof, then uneasy when she realised it was bait.

qa.q: What did Keerthana and Amma do right away?
qa.a: They blocked and reported the player and changed the password.

qa.q: What was the player hoping Keerthana would do?
qa.a: The player hoped the huge number would rush Keerthana into sending her password before thinking or asking anyone.

grounding: A girl is offered free gems for her password, sees it as a warning sign, refuses and tells a trusted adult at once.

passage:
"Mahima didi, someone in my game wants to send me a real gift!"
"What kind of gift?"
"A card with 2000 gems. He just needs our home address to post it."
Mahima put down her book. "Show me."
Deepak turned the phone round. "See? He says I'm lucky. Only five players got picked."
"Deepak, does that feel lucky or strange?"
He chewed his lip. "Bit strange. Why would a stranger want our address?"
"Exactly. Did you send anything?"
"No. I was about to."
"Then you're safe. Come, let's tell Papa right now."
In the next room Papa read the chat, blocked and reported the player with Deepak, and put an arm round him. "Thank you for bringing it straight to us. Offers like this are a trick, not luck."

qa.q: What did the player say was needed to post the card?
qa.a: Their home address.

qa.q: How did Deepak's feelings change as he talked to Mahima?
qa.a: He started out excited and lucky, then grew uneasy and suspicious about why a stranger wanted the address.

qa.q: What did Papa do once he saw the chat?
qa.a: He blocked and reported the player with Deepak and thanked him for bringing it straight to them.

qa.q: Why might the player have told Deepak that only five players were picked?
qa.a: To make Deepak feel special and rushed, so he would send the address without asking anyone.

grounding: A boy offered gems in exchange for his address senses a trick, sends nothing and tells a parent straight away.

passage:
Yogesh and Nakul lived two floors apart in a Kolkata housing colony and checked the weekly game leaderboard every evening. Rank 14, rank 13: they chased each other up the list, shouting through the stairwell.
On Friday Nakul jumped to rank 9. Yogesh stared at his own number, 11, and felt his jaw lock. When Nakul knocked to play cricket, Yogesh said, "Busy," and shut the door.
His sister Himani found him glaring at the screen, replaying the same level. "You've lost five times in a row," she said. "Maybe stop?"
Yogesh put the phone face down. The flat felt very quiet. He thought of Nakul standing outside with the bat.
He ran down two flights. "Still playing?" Nakul grinned and tossed him the ball.

qa.q: What rank did Nakul reach on Friday?
qa.a: Rank 9.

qa.q: What do Yogesh's locked jaw and his "Busy" suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was jealous and sulky about Nakul passing him on the leaderboard.

qa.q: What helped Yogesh stop sulking?
qa.a: Putting the phone face down after Himani's nudge, then running down to play cricket with Nakul.

qa.q: How might Nakul have felt when Yogesh shut the door on him?
qa.a: Nakul was probably confused and a little hurt, since he had come to play, but he still welcomed Yogesh back.

grounding: A boy in a fierce ranking race with his friend starts sulking, takes a break and remembers the friend matters more than the score.

passage:
"Tarun, what's your score?"
"Two thousand four hundred. Beat that, Uma."
"Ha! Two thousand four hundred and fifty!"
"No way. Rematch. Now."
They played again, hunched on Tarun's bed. Tarun won by ten points. Uma tossed her phone onto the pillow.
"This game is rigged."
"It's not rigged, you just lost," Tarun laughed.
"Stop laughing!" Her voice came out sharp. Tarun went quiet and looked at his hands.
Uma looked at his face, then at the phone. "Sorry. I'm getting way too cross about points."
"Me too, sometimes. Yesterday I nearly threw my phone."
"Let's take a break. Your mum said there's mango ice cream."
"Loser serves?"
Uma laughed. "Fine. Loser serves. 😅"

qa.q: By how many points did Tarun win the rematch?
qa.a: By ten points.

qa.q: Why did Uma toss her phone and call the game rigged?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and cross about losing, so she blamed the game.

qa.q: What did Uma do once she noticed her anger, and why did it help?
qa.a: She apologised and suggested a break for ice cream, which put the friendship above the score.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Uma snapped at him?
qa.a: Tarun was likely startled and a bit hurt, going quiet, and then relieved when she said sorry.

grounding: Two friends compete hotly for game scores; when one snaps after losing, she apologises and takes a break to protect the friendship.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5B
For two weeks Bhupen has drawn game maps in the margins of his maths notebook and asked me several times a day when school ends. During silent reading he whispered level names to himself. On Tuesday his mother told me he cried and kicked a chair when the tablet was switched off.
Today I asked him what he misses about the game. He said, "Everything. I think about it all the time." Then, quietly: "It makes my head buzz."
I phoned his parents after school. We agreed they will sit down with him and set game times together. I also asked Arohi, who captains the kho-kho team, to pick him at lunch break. He ran the whole break and came back red-faced and smiling.

qa.q: What did Bhupen draw in the margins of his maths notebook?
qa.a: Game maps.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's "It makes my head buzz" suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels restless and a bit overwhelmed, as if the game has too strong a grip on his mind.

qa.q: What steps did the class teacher take next?
qa.a: They phoned his parents to agree on game times set together with him, and asked Arohi to pick him for kho-kho at lunch.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Bhupen joining the kho-kho team?
qa.a: Arohi probably sees a keen new runner who played the whole break, not just a boy who talks about a game.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a boy who thinks about a game all day and gets upset when it stops, and the agreed limits and outdoor play that help.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today in the science test I read the word "crystals" and my brain shouted CAVE LEVEL. I lost my place twice.
At home Amma said "dinner" and I yelled "ONE MINUTE" about six times. Then I cried when she switched off the wifi. Even I was surprised how angry I got. 😅
After dinner Amma sat on my bed. She wasn't cross. We wrote a deal on paper: game only after homework, forty minutes on school days, then outside. I stuck it on the fridge with the mango magnet.
At six Reena rang the bell for badminton. I almost said no. I went. We played till the streetlights came on, and I forgot the cave level for a whole hour.
Kalyani

qa.q: What did Kalyani and Amma write on the paper?
qa.a: A deal: game only after homework, forty minutes on school days, then outside.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel about the anger when the wifi went off?
qa.a: Kalyani felt surprised and a bit embarrassed at how angry stopping the game made them.

qa.q: What helped loosen the game's grip?
qa.a: The deal made together with Amma, and saying yes to badminton with Reena even when tempted to stay in.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt sitting on Kalyani's bed after the shouting?
qa.a: Amma was likely concerned rather than cross, and wanted to make a plan together instead of fighting.

grounding: A child who thinks about a game at school and gets upset at stopping agrees on time limits with a parent and balances it with outdoor play.

passage: Deepika, come, stop scowling. You shouted at your Ammi about the game? Let me tell you what your Khala did at your age. Our family had one old computer, and I was mad about an online racing game. One evening my Ammi, your Nani, called, "Parveen, switch it off, now!" I was on the last lap. I screamed, "I'm at the most important part!" She walked over and pulled the plug. I lost the whole race and shouted so loudly the neighbours heard. The next day, when we had both cooled down, Ammi said, "Tell me before you start how long a race is." So we agreed: I would say "one race" first, finish it, and get up. Most days it worked, and the shouting stopped.

qa.q: What did Nani do when young Parveen screamed about the last lap?
qa.a: She walked over and pulled the plug.

qa.q: Why did young Parveen scream at Ammi?
qa.a: Parveen felt angry and frustrated at being interrupted on the last lap.

qa.q: Which choice in Khala's story ended the fights, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing before starting to play one race and then get up; nobody was cut off mid-race, so there was less to shout about.

qa.q: How might Parveen's Ammi have seen the moment she pulled the plug?
qa.a: She probably felt ignored and fed up after calling, and wanted to be listened to.

grounding: An aunt recalls shouting at her mother for interrupting a game and how agreeing on "one race" beforehand kept the peace.

passage:
The auto was already honking outside when Seema called, "Akash, phone off, we're leaving for the wedding!"
"Mumma, I'm at the boss level! Two minutes!" Akash shouted without looking up.
"The driver is waiting. Now!"
"You ALWAYS do this!" He threw a cushion. Seema's jaw tightened, and she took the phone and switched it off. Akash sulked through the whole ride, arms folded, his new kurta scratching his neck.
At the wedding he watched his cousins laughing and felt silly. On the drive back he mumbled, "Sorry for shouting. Next time can you tell me earlier? Then I'll finish the round and stop."
Seema squeezed his hand. "Deal. A warning at ten minutes, then off."

qa.q: Where was the family going when Seema called Akash?
qa.a: To a wedding.

qa.q: How did Akash feel watching his cousins laugh at the wedding?
qa.a: He felt silly and a bit ashamed of his shouting and sulking.

qa.q: What plan did Akash and Seema agree on?
qa.a: A warning at ten minutes, so Akash can finish the round and then stop.

qa.q: How did Seema see the moment Akash threw the cushion?
qa.a: Seema, rushed by the honking auto, felt tense and fed up, so she took the phone.

grounding: A boy shouts at his mother for interrupting a game, then agrees on an early warning so he can finish the round and stop.

passage:
"Nilesh, look! The golden armour's on sale, only two hours left!"
"How much?"
"Ninety-nine rupees. Everyone in my team has it. I look like a beginner without it."
"Didn't you want a glowing sword last month too?"
"This is different. It says 'Buy now, don't miss out!'"
"It always says that."
Sarika frowned. "It does?"
"Every week. They put a timer so you panic."
"Oh." She watched the numbers ticking down. "Mummy's card is saved on the tablet. I could just tap."
"Then ask Mummy first."
Sarika carried the tablet to the balcony. Mummy listened and said, "Let's leave it today. If you still want it next week, we'll talk it over together."
Sarika sighed, then shrugged. "Pakhi never even looks at what I'm wearing anyway."

qa.q: How much time did the sale timer say was left?
qa.a: Only two hours.

qa.q: Why did Sarika want the golden armour so badly?
qa.a: She felt left out and a little embarrassed, like a beginner, because her team already had it.

qa.q: What made Sarika slow down before spending?
qa.a: Nilesh pointed out that the timer comes back every week to make players panic, and she asked Mummy first.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see the sale timer?
qa.a: Nilesh sees it as a trick that returns every week to make players panic and tap.

grounding: A girl pressured by a game's timed offer to look cool pauses, asks a parent before spending, and remembers friends don't care about outfits.

passage:
I'm Jasleen. Last month a game I love started showing a shiny panda outfit every time I lost a level. "Win faster with Panda Power!" it flashed. After a few days I truly believed I couldn't win without it. I even counted my birthday money in my head.
Then I noticed something. The pop-up came right after I lost, every single time, when I felt worst. That wasn't luck; somebody planned it that way.
I asked Papa before buying anything, and he said to wait a week and see if I still wanted it. I also asked my friend Chetan if my plain outfit looked silly. He laughed. "I never even noticed what you wear. I just like racing you." I never bought the panda.

qa.q: When did the panda outfit pop-up appear?
qa.a: Right after Jasleen lost a level, every single time.

qa.q: What was Jasleen worried about before talking to Chetan?
qa.a: Jasleen was worried the plain outfit looked silly and felt unable to win without the panda.

qa.q: Which steps helped Jasleen resist the pressure?
qa.a: Noticing the pop-up was timed for the worst moments, asking Papa before buying, and checking with Chetan.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Jasleen's outfit?
qa.a: Chetan does not care about it at all; racing together is what matters.

grounding: A child notices a game's purchase offers are designed to tempt, asks a parent before spending and learns a real friend doesn't care about skins.
